result:
The final answer is in `final.py`. **Search score: 0.5836, against 0.365 for LRU. I used 15 of the 24 scorer calls**, and about 12 of the 15 minutes I announced at the start.

| | search score (scorer) | my harness, tuning seeds | my harness, held-out seeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (LRU) | 0.365 | 0.5055 | 0.4780 |
| First answer (W-TinyLFU, fixed 1% window) | 0.5034 | 0.4733 | – |
| **Final (`final.py`)** | **0.5836** | 0.6057 | 0.5603 |

There was no official held-out split, so the held-out numbers come from seeds of my own trace generator. That generator is only an approximation: it ranked the first answer below LRU, while the scorer ranked it well above. For the last few choices I also looked at those held-out seeds, so they are not a fully clean check.

**How it works.** It is a single cache that can run as either of two policies:
- **LIRS**, which handles loops slightly larger than the cache and one-off scans well.
- **W-TinyLFU**, a small recent-items area in front of a main area that admits a new key only if it has been requested more often than the key it would push out. This wins on hot keys mixed with scans.

13 shadow copies simulate fixed settings of both policies: 5 LIRS sizes, and 3 window sizes × 2 forgetting speeds for TinyLFU. The shadows track only which keys they would hold. Every quarter-capacity requests, the real cache adopts the shadow with the best recent hit rate. It only switches when that shadow leads by a margin: 2% within a policy, 5% across policies. That margin was worth about +0.01 on my harness, because switching back and forth was costing hits. When it changes policy, it rebuilds its structure from the keys it already holds, so it never adds a key that wasn't just requested.

The result is close to the best single policy on every trace type: recency 0.85 (W-TinyLFU alone got 0.60), shifting loops 0.83 (LRU-like policies get 0.16–0.30), and the best scores so far on hot_with_scans (0.248), mixed (0.277) and loop_and_hot (0.660).

**Runtime risk.** An all-new-keys trace of 60k requests takes about 1.2s locally. The scorer runs passed inside its 8-second limit, but if the unseen traces are much longer, that limit is the thing to watch.

**What I tried** (backlog in `backlog.md`, full log in `log.md`):

| Candidate | Search score | Result |
|---|---|---|
| ARC | 0.407 | weak on loops |
| S3-FIFO | 0.440 | |
| W-TinyLFU, window resized by hill-climbing | 0.513 | |
| W-TinyLFU, window resized by ghost hits (ARC-style) | 0.419 | collapses on loops |
| W-TinyLFU, window picked by shadows | 0.5465 | |
| … plus forgetting speed picked by shadows (3 then 10, 30 × capacity) | 0.5545 → 0.5629 | |
| Plain LIRS | 0.5669 | |
| LIRS with HIR (cold-entry) share picked by shadows | 0.5777 | |
| Hybrid LIRS ↔ TinyLFU | 0.5837 | |

Harness only, all no better or worse:
- Admission tweaks: admitting on ties, sampling the victim with the lowest count, capping counters at 15, continuous-decay counts.
- Wider grids: protected share as a shadow dimension, more forgetting speeds, a larger TinyLFU grid inside the hybrid.
- Untuned leftovers: 2Q, LFU with dynamic aging, LeCaR, CLOCK-Pro.

The last change, keeping LIRS's history at 6× capacity instead of 3×, tied on the scorer (0.58364 vs 0.58366). I kept it because it was better on both harness splits.

The scratch candidates, `harness.py`, `brk.py`, `sweep.py`, `log.md` and `backlog.md` are all in the same folder.
